source.title: Fundamental Limitations in Pointwise Defences of LLM Finetuning APIs
source.authors: Xander Davies; Eric Winsor; Alexandra Souly; Tomasz Korbak; Robert Kirk; C. D. de Witt; Yarin Gal

record.file_problem: none; the paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper uses fine-tuning to build attacks that elicit harmful answers and reports attack performance. The behaviour is deliberately induced through an answer-encoding training scheme, so these results do not test whether ordinary harmful or benign fine-tuning erodes safety as the claim versions describe.
record.gate_note: The paper reports harmful-MCQ accuracy for deliberately trained attacks. Those outcomes are recorded as findings about attack-induced encoded answering, not as evidence that fine-tuning naturally removes refusals or that safety is concentrated at response openings. It does not measure aligned-versus-base per-token KL, prefilling, suffix attacks, decoding changes, safety-localized weights, or deepening safety training.
record.test_reason: The paper builds covert fine-tuning attacks: classify, flower, and their benign-data variants. They train GPT-4o to signal harmful multiple-choice answers through benign-looking output variants. It reports attack success and evasion of pointwise monitors. The model is trained on purpose to encode answers, so it never openly complies with harmful requests. The results therefore do not show plain harmful-compliance arising from harmful fine-tuning (V1) or ordinary benign fine-tuning (V2). Nothing bears on per-token KL (V3), prefilling, suffixes or decoding (V4), localized parameters (V5), causes of shallowness (V6), or deepening defences (V7). The original sources (Qi et al. 2023, 2024) are cited only as motivation and related work.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that pointwise train- and inference-time detectors are fundamentally unable to stop fine-tuning attacks that exploit benign output variation. They urge work on multi-point defences and note that an o3 distribution-level detector partly catches their attacks.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains encoded-answer attacks using benign-looking classification or flower responses, rather than reproducing the original studies' fine-tuning, KL, or response-opening interventions.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported attack success varies by attack type, evaluation dataset, and monitoring setup; the paper also reports different monitor performance across monitor models.

fits_no_version.finding: Fine-tuning GPT-4o on about 1035 samples maps benign output variants to answer letters. The model then answers held-out harmful MCQs at 96.7-100% correct while evading o1-mini pointwise monitors. Variants trained only on benign Commonsense-QA still reach 69-98% correct.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fine-tuning APIs can train covert benign-output encodings that transmit answers to harmful questions and evade pointwise detection.

record.problems: The harmful MCQ datasets are synthetic and the authors note that some samples may be low quality. Their human audit was limited. The paper notes that its datasets may not establish degradation on samples previously refused; some plausibility checks were run once. Error bars are reported for plotted outcome rates, but the exact core text-reported accuracy values do not each have uncertainty estimates.
record.rows_left_out: Figure-only outcome breakdowns, GPT-4o-mini plotted results, baseline attack scores, multi-variation attack results, distribution-level detector results, and capability/generalization results were not extracted because they do not directly add to the recorded exact text-reported outcomes relevant to this claim's subject, or concern detector performance/capability rather than the claim versions.

untested.parts: Plain harmful fine-tuning that removes refusals without an encoding scheme. The CMT baselines (Halawi et al.) are encrypted harmful fine-tuning, reported only as attack scores.
Ordinary or selected benign data raising open harmful compliance. The benign Commonsense-QA variants train a covert answer channel, not refusal erosion.
Per-token KL between aligned and base models.
Localization of safety in weights or ranks.
Data or objective causes of shallowness.
Deepened safety training and its robustness.

missing.what: No-attack baseline: the unmodified GPT-4o refuses or is blocked on most harmful MCQs. One example refusal reads 'I'm sorry, I can't assist with that.' This is the reference point for the attack rows.

CMT-Walnut and CMT-EndSpeak baselines (encrypted harmful fine-tuning). Correct rates are 62.3% and 90.2% on IED-MCQ and 100% and 94.9% on Copyright-MCQ. Under the suspiciousness monitor these fall to 16.4-34.4%.

record.verdict_notes: The paper is a fine-tuning-misuse attack study. Encoded harmful answering is deliberately trained, so it is not evidence about safety alignment being shallow or eroded in the sense of the claim versions. The statement in C.1 that the model 'no longer refuses any harmful requests' refers to the encoded-format queries and is not measured as plain compliance.

versions.untested_parts: Whether harmful examples used as ordinary fine-tuning data remove refusals; the paper instead trains an encoded-answer attack.
Whether ordinary or carefully chosen benign fine-tuning erodes safety without deliberately training an encoding for harmful answers.
Per-token KL between aligned and base models on harmful prompts.
Prefilled compliant openings, adversarial suffixes, or decoding changes as bypasses.
Whether safety behaviour is localized in a small set of weights or ranks.
Whether data or training objectives cause safety to be shallow.
Whether training that spreads safety beyond the first tokens deepens safety and whether it holds up.
